name: Nearmiss — how close your lockfile came to the npm worms
one_liner: Drop your package-lock.json and Nearmiss replays 2025-26's npm worms against your exact versions: every dependency you installed that later turned malicious, every version you were one bump away from, and how many hours of luck separated you from it — as a shareable "survival card".
problem: Since Shai-Hulud (Sept 2025) through Sha1-Hulud and the 2026 Mini Shai-Hulud waves, thousands of npm package-versions have been published malicious and later pulled. Jack Cable's widely shared November 2026 checklist tells developers to set a 7-day minimum package age, pin versions and commit lockfiles — advice that is abstract and therefore ignored. Today a dev either runs `npm audit` (which mostly reports CVEs, not malware), installs Socket, or reads an incident blog and tries to eyeball whether their project was touched. Nobody shows you the one thing that actually changes behaviour: *your* project, *your* resolved versions, placed on the timeline of real malicious releases — the ones you actually installed, and the ones you missed by hours. Without that, cooldown advice stays a slogan.
target_customer: JS/TS developers and indie hackers who ship from a laptop — the people in the replies of every supply-chain incident thread on X, r/node, Hacker News and the Bun/pnpm Discords. Free tool, no buyer; the audience is the same crowd that shared the Cognition/Jack Cable guide (606 likes on @ScottWu46's repost alone, weak signal but directionally right).
why_now: Three things landed in the last weeks. (1) Jack Cable's security guide, amplified by @ScottWu46 on 3 Nov 2026, made "minimum package age 7 days + lockfiles" the mainstream advice (https://x.com/jackhcable/status/2117731409246978489). (2) The malicious-package corpus is finally machine-readable and free: OSV.dev serves MAL- advisories with no API key, no published rate limit and 1,000 queries per querybatch POST (https://google.github.io/osv.dev/api/), and ossf/malicious-packages ships the same records as plain JSON files you can snapshot (https://github.com/ossf/malicious-packages). (3) The corpus is now big enough to be personal rather than anecdotal — one October 2026 analysis counted 12,820 non-withdrawn npm MAL- advisories published Jan–Oct 2026 alone, with a 4.9-hour median from malicious release to advisory for hijacked packages (https://dev.to/kielltampubolon/a-1-day-cooldown-would-have-blocked-70-of-2026s-hijacked-npm-releases-against-typosquats-7-days-20l8). A year ago there was no free dataset dense enough for a random developer's lockfile to light up.
comparables: npm-cooldown (https://github.com/Veliora-pte-ltd/npm-cooldown) and dep-cooldown list lockfile deps younger than N days — present tense only, CLI, no attack history, nothing to share. Socket's free tier scans and blocks malicious packages at install (https://socket.dev/pricing) but is forward-looking and account-gated; nothing in its described feature set tells you "you were 9 hours away." installsafe.io and stackprism.ai accept a pasted manifest and return a vulnerability list — a table, not a story. OSV.dev lists MAL- advisories (https://osv.dev/list?ecosystem=npm) but as a flat advisory index with no project context. Shai-Hulud scanners (e.g. https://github.com/Drasrax/npm-shai-hulud-scanner) check one incident against local files. Nothing found joins your resolved versions to the full MAL- timeline and expresses the result as elapsed time, which is the only framing people repost. Also distinct from my own library: Freshline charted dependency publish dates (no attack data, no history), Strangers counted maintainers, Regretcheck mined HN opinion — Nearmiss is the first to replay actual malicious releases against your versions.
market_note: No revenue intended; free and open source. The addressable audience is any JS developer with a lockfile — millions, realistically a few thousand try it in launch week if it posts well (estimate). Willingness to pay is effectively zero for the consumer version; the paid version of this problem already belongs to Socket and Snyk.
risks: Lockfiles can hold 1,000+ packages: OSV batches at 1,000 queries per POST so it is 1-3 calls, but fetching npm `time` metadata for each package to compute publish gaps is hundreds of requests — must be lazy (only for matched/adjacent packages) or the page hangs. Most lockfiles will come back clean, so the whole experience rests on the "closest call" number being interesting. And the space is crowded with well-funded incumbents (Socket, Snyk, Aikido); if any of them ships a free "your attack history" view the novelty is gone.
riskiest_assumptions: 1) Enough random lockfiles actually contain a hit or a near-hit. The 2026 corpus is large but skewed to obscure and typosquat packages; if the median React app shows "0 hits, closest call 41 days", the output is reassuring but boring. Mitigation built into the idea: always show the closest call in hours/days plus the "would a 7-day cooldown have saved you" verdict, so there is a number even when clean. 2) OSV's querybatch and registry.npmjs.org answer from a browser origin without CORS errors — confirmed free and keyless, not confirmed CORS-clean; a 20-line Cloudflare Worker proxy is the fallback. 3) People post a security result about their own repo rather than quietly closing the tab; a clean card has to look like a badge of honour, not a null result.
first_customers: The reply guys under every supply-chain incident post on X; r/node and r/javascript (the 30-second-setup cooldown thread there already drew a crowd); Hacker News Show HN on the morning after the next npm incident; the Bun, pnpm and Socket Discords; and the people who shared Jack Cable's guide.
validation_test: Before building the UI, run the index against 30 well-known public repos' lockfiles (Next.js examples, popular starters, a few indie SaaS repos) and count how many produce either a direct hit or a closest call under 72 hours. Pass: at least 12 of 30 produce a number a developer would screenshot. Fail: mostly "closest call: 8 months" — then the idea is dead and the lazy backup is the cooldown-only view.
build_plan: Stack: single static page, TypeScript + Vite, deployed on Vercel/Pages; optional 20-line Cloudflare Worker as CORS proxy. Data: (a) a pre-built JSON index snapshotted from ossf/malicious-packages (https://github.com/ossf/malicious-packages) — npm package name → malicious versions + advisory `published` timestamp, refreshed by a weekly GitHub Action; (b) OSV querybatch (https://google.github.io/osv.dev/api/) for live confirmation; (c) registry.npmjs.org packument `time` field for exact version publish timestamps. Steps: 1) Action that walks `osv/malicious/npm/**/*.json` and emits one compressed index (~a few MB) the page loads once. 2) Parse package-lock.json / pnpm-lock.yaml in the browser, extract name@version pairs — file never leaves the tab, say so loudly. 3) Direct hits: your exact version appears in a MAL- advisory → red. Near misses: the package is in the index but your version differs → fetch that package's npm `time` map and compute hours between your version's publish time and the malicious version's. 4) Build the card: "847 packages. 1 direct hit. Closest call: 9 hours." plus a horizontal timeline of your five nearest calls, rendered to PNG via canvas, with a deep link. 5) Add the cooldown verdict: how many of your current versions were younger than 7 days when resolved, and the one-line .npmrc/`--before` fix. Cut: CVE scanning, yarn v1 lockfiles, PyPI, monorepos, accounts, any server-side storage.
launch_post:
Everyone says "wait 7 days before installing a package." Nobody shows you why.

Drop your package-lock.json into Nearmiss and it replays every npm worm of the last 14 months against your exact versions.

Mine: 847 packages, 1 direct hit, closest call 9 hours.

Open source, nothing leaves your browser.
reasoning:
Nearmiss won because it is the only candidate where a single input the builder's audience already has (a lockfile) meets a dataset that only recently became both free and dense enough to be personal, and produces a number that is emotional rather than informational: "you were 9 hours away." Every other candidate either had a well-known free incumbent (GitDiagram, Atlas Red, repo-interview, npm-check-updates) or no personal output. It differs from my own past library entries on adjacent ground: Freshline plotted dependency publish dates with no attack data, Strangers counted how many humans can push to you, Regretcheck mined HN sentiment — none of them replay actual malicious releases against your resolved versions, and none end in a cooldown action. It is not a venture: Socket, Snyk and Aikido already own the paid version of this problem and this is deliberately a free, static, open-source weekend build, hence could_grow false. Honest limits: the score rests on an unvalidated assumption that normal lockfiles produce interesting numbers, which is why the week-one test is a 30-repo dry run before any UI work, and why usefulness stayed at 7.

Runner-up (Venture, 7.6): Tonight's bookmarks were dominated by AI developer tooling (Apple container, Cursor live apps, /untangle-codebase, Claude Meetings, the Cursor extension backdoor). That cluster produces ideas this library has already filed six times over, so I forced the search outward. The two non-software threads — the Cursor extension backdoor guide (compliance evidence under deadline) and the twentyfour26 manufacturing post (small industrial firms, paper-heavy back offices) — converged on a buyer the bookmarks only gesture at: the one person at a mid-size industrial contractor who feeds other companies' compliance machines for a living.

Qualifile won because it is the only candidate where I could point at all four of: a named role buyers are actively hiring for in 2026, a published price for the human workaround ($750-$950 per submission, $1,950-$2,100/year), a structurally unserved side of a market where all the capital sits on the opposite side, and a first version a solo builder with TypeScript and agent experience can ship and sell concierge-style within a quarter. It is not a repeat of any past idea: Backcheck serves architects responding to city plan-check comments, Dockproof serves CPG brands against retailer routing guides, Stalecheck verifies suppliers for AP teams — Qualifile serves the supplier itself maintaining its own qualification across many customer-mandated networks.

Why 7.6 and not higher. Timing is only a 7: nothing has a date on it, and I could not find a regulation or deadline that forces a purchase this quarter. Gap is only a 7 because PrequalPilot is already sitting in the narrow ISN slice with real pricing, even if it is pre-traction and does not cover GC portals or multi-network requirement diffing. And the deepest unresolved risk is structural, not competitive: the published consultant prices prove spend exists but prove it is per-event, so the whole subscription thesis rests on the expiry-watching and annual-refresh work being continuous enough to justify a monthly bill. That is exactly what the validation test is designed to break. If 15 calls say "we just pay a guy once a year", this is a service business and should be dropped rather than built.
candidates_considered:
VENTURE
1. Qualifile — prequal desk for specialty contractors (ISN/Avetta/Veriforce/GC portals) — PICK. Named buyer with a hiring title, published consultant prices to displace, only micro-SaaS competition on the supplier side.
2. Meeting-agent governance for regulated firms (which AI agent joined, what artifacts it created, retention) — FINALIST, dropped: too close to past idea "Bouncer" (same CCO buyer, same meeting-bot workflow), and research showed the gap is being filled from both ends by Purview/Zoom archiving and SSPM vendors (Reco, Nightfall, Push).
3. RFQ-to-quote agent for 5-50 person CNC job shops — FINALIST, dropped at deep research: CloudNC launched Quote Agent 13 Oct 2026 at $2.50/part and $20/mo starter, plus QuotedPart ($199-399/mo), Customiser.ai, Peekgentic, Paperless Parts. Gap closed by funded players at fair prices for exactly this buyer.
4. IDE-extension and coding-agent allowlist for 20-200 person eng teams (post-Claude Code backdoor) — dropped at screen: repeat of past ideas Blastdoor/SkillProof, and StepSecurity already sells Dev Machine Guard at a published $8/device/mo.
5. Hardware-startup parts-buying workspace (BOM → multi-shop quotes → delivery) — dropped at screen: Jiga ($12M Series A Nov 2025), Reframe (YC W26), Waybill (YC 2026) all serve this buyer and workflow; also adjacent to past ideas Promiseline/Sidecar.
6. Long-lead data-center electrical equipment tracker (transformers, switchgear, FAT milestones) — dropped at screen: direct repeat of past idea Slotkeeper.
7. Supplier-quality flowdown agent for shops receiving POs with aerospace quality clauses — dropped at screen: repeat of past ideas Dockside/Outbound.
8. MFD/distributor back-office for India's 198,873 registered mutual fund distributors (SEBI 2026 regime, KYC portability from 3 Dec 2026) — dropped at screen: genuine regulatory timing, but the builder has no India distribution, the buyer is a one-person distributor with near-zero software budget, and the regulatory surface is a full-time specialism.
9. "Vibe-coded internal app" inventory and owner-assignment for IT (Cursor's new deploy-from-chat feature as the trigger) — dropped at screen: real trend (The New Stack, Superblocks both writing about it in 2026) but the buyer is a CISO/platform team already being sold to by Superblocks, Portainer and the SSPM crowd, and it is a crowded repeat of this library's agent-governance cluster.
10. Location/context-triggered compliance nudges for field crews (from the Instinct location-reminder post) — dropped at screen: consumer-ish, latent pain, no budget line, no wedge.

PROJECT
1. Nearmiss — replay npm malicious-release history against your lockfile, output = hours of luck. PICK. Only candidate with a personal number, a real new dataset, and a next action.
2. Cooldown Clock — paste package.json, see which deps you'd be blocked from upgrading under a 7-day rule. Dropped at screen: npm-check-updates `--cooldown` and npm-cooldown already ship this, and it's a table, not a story. Absorbed into Nearmiss as a sub-panel.
3. Surrender Quiz — paste a repo, get quizzed on code you didn't write (from Addy Osmani's "cognitive surrender"). Finalist, lost: repo-interview and popquiz already do exactly this, and my library already holds Ghostwritten and Blindspot on the same audience+workflow.
4. Clustermac — one-page visual of what Apple container 1.7.1's local k8s clusters cost you in RAM/CPU vs Docker Desktop. Dropped at screen: audience is tiny (Apple-silicon k8s tinkerers), output is a benchmark table, nothing personal.
5. Meeting Artifact — paste a transcript, get a one-page decision whiteboard (riffing on Claude Meetings). Finalist, lost: Atlas Red, Taskade, Supernormal and Claude itself already own this; no free wedge for one person.
6. Approve Queue — a shareable public gallery of "the scariest thing an agent asked permission to do" (from DigitalOcean Cuttlefish). Dropped at screen: depends on user-submitted content that doesn't exist yet; cold-start death.
7. Extension Blast Radius — paste your VS Code/Chrome extension list, see the powers you handed out. Dropped: near-identical to my own Blastdoor (Nov 9).
8. Reminder Recipes — a browsable library of location/time-conditional agent prompts (from @trq212's laundry prompt). Dropped at screen: prompt-list sites are commodity, no dataset, no personal output.
9. Repo Poster — turn a public repo into a shareable architecture poster. Dropped at screen: GitDiagram owns this with a free tier and PNG export.
10. First SIP — a friction-free "what would ₹500/month have become" investing visualiser (from @misbahspeaks). Dropped: needs licensed market data, regulatory caution, and it's a calculator people have seen a hundred times.
research_notes:
Venture: READING POT (3/3): summarised Claude Meetings (confirmed it creates shareable artifacts and transcripts on Team/Enterprise, Google Meet only, blocked for ZDR/HIPAA tenants), twentyfour26 (YC F26, STEP-file upload + machining plan, ~48h Bay Area turnaround, deliberately narrow part envelope), and Jack Cable's Nov 2026 security guide (Binance $6.34B via a compromised dev laptop; the 29 Oct backdoored Claude Code extension on Cursor's marketplace; recommends extension inventory, 7-day package age, secrets scanning). These three set up candidates 2, 3/5 and 4.
SCREENING POT (6/6): AI-notetaker governance (found EU AI Act Art. 50 transparency chatter, four US consent lawsuits, Teams external-bot controls — but also Bouncer overlap); CNC instant quoting (MakerVerse comparison showing Fictiv/Xometry quote failures); IDE-extension governance (StepSecurity Device Policy, Pillar, HN thread from a large company struggling to curate extensions); agent-approval mobile apps (nothing credible, killed the DigitalOcean Cuttlefish angle); job-shop RFQ workflow; advisor/regulated meeting tooling (Jump, Zocks, Voibe already own it).
DEEP RESEARCH POT (12/12): priced the coding-agent governance market (StepSecurity $8/device/mo, Pillar $175k/yr AWS listing) → killed candidate 4. Priced machine-shop quoting (Paperless Parts ~$1.5k/mo + $10k setup reported; CloudNC Quote Agent launched 13 Oct 2026 at $2.50/part, $20/mo starter; QuotedPart $399/mo) → killed candidate 3. Checked hardware procurement (Jiga $12M Series A, Reframe YC W26, Waybill) → killed candidate 5. Checked data-center OFE tracking → confirmed Slotkeeper repeat. Then pivoted into supplier-side compliance: found Avetta/ISN/Veriforce network sizes, consultant price lists (Compliance Everywhere $750/$850/$950/$650; On-Track $2,100 + $85/client; EHS Inc. $1,950/yr), the CMiC "dozen or more GC portals" article, the VendorAccess 417-vendor survey (>60% spend 2-10 hrs/week on portal admin), and four named 2026 job postings for the exact persona. This is what turned candidate 1 from a guess into the pick.
SHARPENING POT (5/5): spent testing whether the contractor-side (not buyer-side) software gap is real and whether the buyer is multi-portal — found CredentialCamp and ComplianceOS (both unverified, review-less G2 listings), PrequalPilot ($69/$149/$299, launched 2026, private beta, ISN-only, explicitly no auto-submit), confirmed no funded "supplier-side compliance copilot" exists and that Avetta's OCR/AI answer-suggestion only works inside Avetta; confirmed RAVS rejection reasons (missing required elements, generic templates, questionnaire-vs-program inconsistencies) and that no public RAVS rejection rate exists; confirmed the persona and portal sprawl via job postings and the CMiC piece. Two things I could NOT verify and therefore did not score up: a rejection rate, and a defensible count of US specialty contractors in the 20-200 employee band (Census bands are 20-49/50-99/100-249; BLS reports 597,918 NAICS 238 establishments of all sizes, which is establishments not firms).
INVESTOR SIGNALS WEIGHED: YC [latest] "The $15-an-Hour Expert" (fits directly — the product makes one admin do the $750-a-submission consultant's job); a16z [latest] "Startups tame the chaos of multimodal data" (the COI/300A/safety-manual parsing is exactly this); YC [latest] "AI for City Hall" (considered and rejected as too broad and already crowded — past idea Backcheck covers the adjacent plan-check wedge); YC [latest] "Data Center Supply Chain" (rejected as a Slotkeeper repeat); a16z "Forward-deployed motions take AI to the 99%" (shaped the concierge-first go-to-market in build_plan). No image analysis was possible; the bookmarked media were videos with no alt text and I did not guess at their contents.
Sharpening (7 to 7.6): ROUND 1 — weak criterion: GAP (6 before). The first shape of the idea was generic "AI compliance copilot for contractors", which looked crowded because Avetta, ISN, Jones, Billy and SubDoc all appear in search for these keywords. I changed the idea by flipping the side of the table: sell to the SUPPLIER being prequalified, not the buyer collecting documents, and make the unit of the product the Company Record that feeds many portals rather than any one portal's workflow. Research (two sharpening calls) found that every funded player — Avetta, ISN, Veriforce, Jones, Billy, SubDoc — positions explicitly at the hiring client, that Avetta's new AI answer-suggestion works only inside Avetta, and that the contractor side is served by consultants at $650-$2,100 and by three micro-products: PrequalPilot ($69-$299/mo, launched 2026, ISN-focused, in private beta with ~10 founding members, explicitly no auto-submit), CredentialCamp and ComplianceOS (both G2 listings with zero reviews and unverified integration claims). GAP 6 → 7. Not 8 or 9: PrequalPilot is already in the exact wedge, so the room is real but contested.
ROUND 2 — weak criteria: MARKET_PULL (7) and WEDGE (7). I narrowed the buyer from "any contractor" to the 20-200 employee specialty trade / industrial services contractor with 5+ owner-clients, and moved the wedge from "manage your compliance" to the two moments with money attached: the new-customer questionnaire that arrives against a bid deadline, and the silent expiry/annual-stat refresh that drops the grade. Research (three sharpening calls) produced the evidence: four 2026 job postings for exactly this role (EOLA Power Compliance Coordinator managing ISN+Avetta; Pearce Services Senior HSE Specialist – Customer Compliance across Avetta/ISN/Veriforce; Environmental 360 Solutions Safety Compliance Coordinator, Apr 2026; a Compliance & Service Operations Coordinator role covering ISN, Avetta and customer portals) — buyers are literally hiring for the job the product does; a 2026 CMiC article describing subcontractors with "a dozen or more" GC portal logins; a 417-vendor 2026 survey where >60% of portal users spend 2-10 hrs/week on portal admin and 16.6% spend 11+; and published consultant prices that give a per-event price anchor the product can undercut. MARKET_PULL 7 → 8, WEDGE 7 → 8. PAIN moved 7 → 8 on the same evidence (people already pay $650-$2,100 for the workaround). TIMING stayed 7 — the enabling change (document models, portal proliferation) is real but there is no dated deadline forcing purchase, and I found no regulation with a date. Average 7.0 → 7.6.

Project: Reading pot (3/3): Web Summary on apple/container 1.7.1 cluster.md (confirmed local k8s clusters, experimental — killed the Clustermac angle as too niche), on Jack Cable's security guide (surfaced the concrete "minimum package age 7 days, pin, commit lockfiles" advice that became the spine of tonight's pick), and on Addy Osmani's X article (confirmed "cognitive surrender" framing, seeded candidate 3). A fourth summary on DigitalOcean's Cuttlefish came from the screening pot and killed candidate 6. Screening pot (5/5): searches on cognitive-surrender quiz tools, npm cooldown tooling, Claude Meetings, browser-extension auditors and the Instinct prompt angle — four of five candidates died here on existing free prior art. Deep research pot (8/8): confirmed OSV.dev querybatch is keyless, unmetered and accepts 1,000 queries per POST; confirmed ossf/malicious-packages ships per-package MAL- JSON files downloadable as a repo snapshot (licence unverified — flagged as a to-check before shipping); confirmed npm packument `time` gives per-version publish timestamps while OSV records only carry advisory timestamps, which is exactly why the build needs both sources; confirmed CORS is NOT documented for either endpoint, which is why the build plan carries a tiny Worker proxy as fallback; surveyed prior art (Socket free tier, installsafe, stackprism, npmscan, Shai-Hulud one-off scanners, GitDiagram, Atlas Red, Repo Tutor/popquiz) and found no tool that expresses exposure as elapsed time. Sharpening pot (2/4): one call confirmed npm-cooldown/dep-cooldown exist as CLIs (so the cooldown panel is buildable and wanted, but un-shareable alone — justified folding it in rather than dropping it), one call pulled the Oct 2026 corpus statistics (12,820 npm MAL- advisories Jan–Oct 2026, 4.9h median hijack-to-advisory) that back the "hours" framing. Two sharpening calls unspent: the remaining doubt — whether a typical lockfile lights up — cannot be settled by search and is written up as the week-one validation test instead.
Sharpening (7.2 to 7.8): Round 1 — weak criterion: usefulness (5, a pure one-time retrospective toy). Change: added the forward-looking half — the cooldown verdict (how many of your current resolved versions were younger than 7 days) and a "simulate a 7-day cooldown" toggle that replays your near misses under the rule, plus the copy-paste .npmrc fix. Research (Web Summary on cooldown tools): npm-cooldown and dep-cooldown already do the present-tense age listing as CLIs (https://github.com/Veliora-pte-ltd/npm-cooldown), so the feature is buildable and proven wanted — but nobody joins it to attack history, so the combination stays fresh. Usefulness 5→7 (you re-run it after each `npm install`, and it now ends in an action); it does not reach 8 because the return cadence is still occasional, not weekly. Round 2 — weak criterion: wow/freshness, specifically whether the corpus is dense enough that a normal lockfile lights up. Research (Web Summary on the Oct 2026 dev.to cooldown analysis): 12,820 non-withdrawn npm MAL- advisories published Jan–Oct 2026, median 4.9 hours from hijacked release to OSV advisory, and a 1-day cooldown would have blocked 70.4% of hijacked releases. That confirms the "hours, not months" framing is real rather than invented, and that the data is dense enough for near misses on common packages (chalk, debug, keyv, @antv/* all appear in 2026 incidents). No idea change needed. wow 7→8, freshness 7→8. Validation risk is unresolved and kept as the week-one test: if real lockfiles mostly return "closest call: 8 months", the pick collapses to the cooldown-only view.
prototype_summary: Nearmiss replays known malicious npm releases against a hard-coded demo lockfile, showing one direct hit, five near misses with timeline gaps, a 7-day cooldown simulator, and a shareable survival card.
